Title: Your Agent Doesn't Need an LLM to Plan
Abstract: Every step your agent takes costs a model call. Plan a twenty-step task, pay twenty times, and get a different plan each run.  That isn't a law of nature. It's an architectural choice, and it's the wrong one.  **GATS** (Graph-Augmented Tree Search) inverts it. Instead of asking a language model what to do next, it runs UCB1 tree search over a persistent state-transition graph the agent builds as it works. The LLM never picks an action. It lives inside *skills*, synthesizing a diff or reading a file, and even there, only when a cheaper layer can't answer.  That escalation ladder is the core idea:  - **L1, symbolic**: preconditions and effects you already know. Free, exact, and it covers most of what an agent does all day. - **L2, learned**: per-state transition statistics mined from the agent's own execution history. Takes over once an action turns out to be stochastic. - **L3, generative**: the LLM proposes effects for genuinely novel actions. The result is cached, so a novel situation costs at most one call, ever.  Episode one pays. Episode two is free. On a 100-task suite: **100% success, 100% optimal plans, zero model calls at plan time, zero variance across runs.**  Then the result I didn't expect. Swap the simulated backend for a real local Llama 3.2 and run the same benchmark: the tree-search baseline collapses from 87% to under 1%, ReAct falls to 36%, and GATS doesn't move, because GATS wasn't calling the model at plan time to begin with. Planning quality stopped being a function of model quality.

Title: Orchestrating AI Agents with Pattern Matching
Abstract: Pattern matching is emerging as a powerful mechanism for bringing structure and determinism into systems built on top of probabilistic AI outputs. In this session, we explore how modern pattern-matching constructs can be used to orchestrate AI agents in a predictable, maintainable, and auditable way.  The talk demonstrates how outputs generated by AI agents, often unstructured and ambiguous, can be transformed into well-defined, typed representations and then routed through pattern-matching logic to drive decision-making. Using practical examples, we show how to implement routing, delegation, retries, fallbacks, and termination flows using pattern-matching constructs available in modern programming languages.  Beyond implementation details, the session introduces a broader architectural perspective: treating AI agents as components in a deterministic system, where pattern matching serves as the control layer that governs behavior. This approach reduces uncertainty, improves traceability, and enables engineers to build systems that are both flexible and reliable.

Title: Beyond the Context Window: Building a "Mental Model" for Your AI Agents
Abstract: We’ve all seen what happens when you give an LLM a single repo: it’s usually quite successful. But what happens when you give it a distributed system with 200 microservices? It gets lost in the "muddy middle". The bottleneck in AI-driven development isn't code generation; it’s architectural context.  This talk introduces the Application Architecture Hub - a living, AI-maintained knowledge base designed specifically for agent consumption.  We will explore how to move away from static, stale documentation and toward a system of automated "facets" (APIs, Domain Models, Events, and more) that allow AI agents to troubleshoot, design, and assess impact across your entire ecosystem. We'll explore how this can benefit workflows beyond coding, across the organization.  Attendees will leave with a blueprint for building an ingestion pipeline that keeps their AI agents (and their humans) in sync with the "truth" of the codebase.

Title: Building Resilient AI Agents: Lessons from Octopus Architecture in Rust
Abstract: Most AI agent frameworks are fragile — one LLM outage brings the entire system down. Octos is a Rust-native AI agent framework inspired by the octopus nervous system, now growing an open-source community around resilience-first agent architecture.  This talk covers: 1. Why current agent architectures fail under provider failures — and why it matters for your users 2. The octopus architecture: one central brain + eight independent arms, mapped from neuroscience to software 3. Three-layer fault tolerance in production: RetryProvider → ProviderChain → AdaptiveRouter across 15 LLM providers 4. Building an open-source community around a resilience-first agent framework — what worked, what didn't 5. Performance that makes self-hosting viable: 31MB binary, <100ms cold start, 200+ concurrent agents on 16GB RAM 6. 100% MIT licensed — zero vendor lock-in, no hidden limits  Attendees will leave with a concrete architecture pattern and community-building insights for resilient, production-grade AI agents.

Abstract: My Goal is show how use , Agno for create deepagents using a lib for this, also sow some resources in Agno, for create agentes with max performance and low use for tokens.  Also show ginga (https://github.com/devalexandre/deep-agent-ginga) a cli created with agno-go a port from agno-python to golang

Title: Agentic patterns for domain driven design
Abstract: As AIOps and collaboration tools pivot toward “agentic” functionality, many teams struggle to move beyond unreliable chat prompts. The challenge isn’t just “calling an LLM”—it’s architecting a system where agents reliably interact with complex domains, respect business logic, and scale alongside existing microservices.  In this session, we explore Agentic Patterns for Domain-Driven Design, drawing on successful implementations from best-of-breed SaaS platforms. We will dissect the three critical layers of a modern agentic stack—Interaction, Orchestration, and Domain—while focusing on the rigorous engineering required to take a project from concept to code.  Key topics include:  The PRD as Prompt Engineering: How to construct a “spec” that drives planning in IDE assistants. We’ll discuss writing requirements that are machine-readable and context-aware to ensure AI-generated code aligns with your architectural standards.  Testing for Quality Attributes: How to move beyond “vibes-based” testing. We will cover technical validation for scalability, identifying tech debt early in AI-generated modules, and the “Token Tax”—how to model cost (COGS) when tokens drive your unit economics.  The Orchestration Plane: A comparison of the Manager-Delegate pattern versus Serial Agent Tasks, and how to manage execution state at scale.  The Domain & Information Layer: Integrating backend microservices via the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and custom RAG to maintain a “clean” architecture.  From MVP to Mainline: Strategies for transferring your agentic project from a rapid-prototype MVP into a normal development cycle, ensuring it inherits the same CI/CD, observability, and security posture as your core platform. More at: https://www.papercall.io/talks/436069

Title: What if you could deploy Azure end-to-end scenarios while sleeping?
Abstract: In my previous role as Technical Trainer at Microsoft, I had to build and deploy a new Azure scenario daily to make my workshops more engaging and reflective of real-customer scenarios. This turned into an Open Source project in 2025, with +75 scenarios to reuse. Building those scenarios was time-intensive, error-prone and just no fun. That's why I flipped it into a full agentic solution. That is still Open-Source for you to reuse and contribute to. If you manage Azure, or you just want to learn more about the platform with actual scenarios to deploy, but you don't want to build them manually, this session is for you!

Title: Riding the AI wave as a fullstack engineer
Abstract: We will be taking a walk through the various tools and techniques for full-stack engineers to leverage the various AI tools to improve efficiency and stay ahead of the curve in the fast paced, growing labyrinth of AI tools and techniques available. The talk will also take a short look at integrating with some of the more populate AI powered coding tools like cloud ai, github copilot and cursor. We will explore how this tool can help developers write and ship maintainable and well tested code faster and easier with real world simple examples. We will also explore some of the intricacies of making client side (frontend) development easier using code generation tools from figma on a minimal level.

Title: Training and deploying an image classifier on a budget: PyTorch, Kaggle, and Hugging Face Spaces
Abstract: A fast, practical walkthrough of training a flower classification model using PyTorch on Kaggle and deploying it as a live application on Hugging Face Spaces — without a GPU cluster or a cloud budget. Covers the full pipeline: dataset preparation, model training, probability-based prediction output, and deployment. Includes the mistakes made along the way and what the process taught about the gap between a working notebook and a working application. For engineers curious about applied ML who want to understand the end-to-end flow before committing to a larger project.

Title: Building Real-Time, Multimodal AI Agents
Abstract: Generative AI often sits isolated in experimental notebooks, disconnected from the high-velocity data of the real world. In this session, we introduce an architecture (Apache NiFi, Apache Iceberg, Claude Models and Apache Kafka) that includes a blueprint for operationalizing AI on data in motion.  We will demonstrate how to move beyond static RAG by building a live "vision agent" that ingests real-time video streams, performs autonomous video, text, audio and image analysis using multimodal LLMs and triggers downstream actions instantly.  Attendees will see a live blueprint where data ingestion, vectorization and inference happen in a unified, serverless loop, turning raw chaos into structured intelligence.  We also should how to enhance code bases, test, validate and document with Agentic Code Tools.  Use Case walk throughs highlight Drone analytics for Insurance, ATM foot traffic analysis and where the real-world collides with streams of financial numerics  Example Full source Code https://github.com/tspannhw/SNACKAI-CoCo-TrafficVideo

Title: My Step Functions DAG Was a Lie: Going Agentic on 8,000 Photos
Abstract: Once I decided to translate my photography experience into a serverless pipeline. I judged 8000 photos of your faces, and it was a big success - we turned a problem into a solution with AWS. Lambdas, Rekognition, Bedrock and the rest played together as a system, delivering a memorable AWS Community Day.  The talk traveled far - but it had a fatal weakness. It was good while it lived in the conference room. Outside, my taste - hardcoded into weights and thresholds, and a single Claude call guessing how to process every file - brought things to disaster. It ran rules I wrote for photographs I hadn't taken yet, and failed silently on every shot that didn't fit. Terraform destroy.  Vérité This year I tore out every guess. With agents.  Imagine swapping the single photographer for the press agency. I'll show how to keep a mature orchestration relevant in the agentic era. How a chain of pipelines became a grid of agents - separate programs, each with its own tooling and skills distilled from real photography craft. Where the agent reasons about what belongs and judges against real craft, not one engineer's gut. Where v1 had a frozen rule, v2 has a program that thinks.  I'll draw the parallels - where we broke through, where classic approaches still win, which weaknesses got replaced and what each agent does instead. You'll leave with a pattern for any rigid pipeline: which box is a guess, and what if it could reason instead?  Last year I automated my hands. This year, my judgment.

Title: From Prompt to Production Dashboard: Agentic AI with MCP Servers and Live Data
Abstract: Description What happens between a user typing "Show me AR aging by customer" and a fully interactive dashboard appearing on screen? This talk pulls back the curtain on a production agentic system that turns natural language into deployed dashboards — complete with KPIs, charts, and filterable tables — powered by live enterprise data.  At the core is a ReAct agent loop that reasons about data needs, discovers available tools at runtime, and iterates through up to 10 cycles of thought-action-observation to produce a structured DashboardSpec. The agent connects to enterprise ERP data through MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers, an open protocol for dynamic tool discovery across multiple transports (SSE and Streamable HTTP), with a Redis caching layer that cuts repeated query latency by 50x.  Dashboards aren't throwaway artifacts — they're versioned resources. An append-only versioning model in Cassandra supports full CRUD, while an edit supervisor agent handles conversational modifications, deciding which components need a data refetch versus a pure visualization change. Every step — tool calls, agent reasoning, validation results, final render — streams to the frontend in real time via GraphQL subscriptions over WebSocket.  The architecture is built on portable, open technologies: LangGraph for agent orchestration, FastAPI for the service layer, and Strawberry GraphQL for the subscription API. No vendor lock-in, no proprietary frameworks.  This is a live demo talk. You'll watch the system handle ambiguous prompts, recover from MCP server failures, and validate outputs through structured tool schemas — then walk away with an architecture pattern you can implement Monday morning.

Title: Less Theater, More Engineering: A Production Claude Code + MCP Agent Pipeline at 80% Accuracy
Abstract: Most agentic AI is theater. This is the inverse — a production agent orchestration pipeline that earned its 80% accuracy through engineering, not vibes. I built an AI pipeline using Claude Code and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) that runs at a Fortune 500 telecom and previously at a top-25 mobile consumer app. Three MCP servers — Confluence/Jira, a structured test-case repository, the automation codebase — let the model translate product requirements into Jira stories, test cases, and executable Appium/TypeScript code at ~80% accuracy.  The talk is about the 20%: where agents drift, why orchestration patterns matter more than model choice, and why the human-in-the-loop PR gate is the feature that makes the system shippable.  Five lessons that earned scars: don't ask the model to do deterministic work — flaky detection drifts; constrain to a JSON schema or review time blows up 5x; the human PR gate is mandatory — a silent regression cost us a multi-week mess; measure quality before optimizing cost — we cut tokens 25% and hotfixes ticked up; don't replace the existing automation runtime, layer agents on top.  The takeaway: ~80% of generated automation runs the intended scenario without post-generation edits. The cheap-fail-to-expensive-fail ratio after guardrails is 4:1 (was 1:1 without). That ratio is the year of work behind this talk.  Attendees leave with: a reference architecture for production agent orchestration, MCP integration patterns, a failure-mode catalog, and a 30/60/90-day adoption plan.

Title: From Prompts to Review Harnesses: Scaling AI Code Reviews Across 70+ Software Projects
Abstract: How do you turn brittle AI prompts into a reliable review process for many software projects? This experience report shows the evolution from prompt-based AI reviews to a deterministic review harness with an agent runner, MCP server, managed checklists, enforced completeness, persisted intermediate results, automated reports, and an interactive result UI.

Title: The Harness Decides What to Trust: Running AI Coding Loops Without Shipping Fiction
Abstract: AI coding does not fail because models are weak. It fails because the system around them trusts the wrong evidence. I will show the harness I use to turn agent output into something shippable: short specs, isolated git worktrees, model routing by role, browser-based verification, screenshot gates, regression hunters, and cost controls. The same operating style powers Ralph Starter, my portfolio build pipeline, and the benchmark loops behind public #1 results. The point is not use more agents. The point is that builders should not grade their own work, a passing build is not proof of a good UI, and every keep decision needs a ruler. Attendees will leave with a practical blueprint for building agent loops that stop on evidence instead of confidence.

Title: Integrating Agentic Workflows: Scaling Engineering Productivity for Uber's Driver Onboarding Team
Abstract: In this session, we’ll dive into a case study on how the Driver Onboarding team transitioned lots of manual, script-heavy engineering processes into agentic-based ones. We’ll explore how various AI agents were integrated into the developer lifecycle to scale team output.  The session will include: - Existing workflows and the pain points associated with them - How the team transitioned those workflows into agentic-based ones - Overview of the AI-based tools and landscape at Uber - Best practices for integrated agentic workflows

Title: Squad Goals: Orchestrating Multi-Agent Engineering Teams in Your Repo
Abstract: Single-agent coding tops out fast. Multi-agent Squad workflows don't. In this practical talk, Marco Antonio Silva introduces Squad: a pattern for planning, review, and merge ceremonies with collaborating agents inside a real repository. Through live demos, attendees see how a crew decomposes work, owns handoffs, gates quality, and recovers from broken builds. Leave knowing when to use a squad instead of one agent and how to bootstrap one on Monday.

Title: Deleting 50,000 Lines of Python: Delegating Complex Migrations to AI Agents
Abstract: Aleksandr Nikolenko shows how to hand off a production traffic migration to an agent and achieve a safer outcome than doing it by hand. The case study: moving search from an old Python service to a new Rust path in under one month, deleting roughly 50,000 lines of Python, and reaching zero traffic on the old service without asking users to discover the regressions. The talk breaks down the contract that made delegation possible: a clear goal, output verification running against real traffic samples, a shadow workspace where the Rust implementation could fail safely, and human gates before traffic moved. Nikolenko also shows what the loop caught that code review alone would have missed: ranking-order divergences across sampled live queries, schema mismatches invisible to unit tests, and the failure mode when no such loop exists: silent regressions waiting for users to discover them.

Title: Building AI-Driven Fabrication Systems for Scalable Infrastructure Delivery
Abstract: How do you successfully deploy AI in an industrial fabrication environment where quality, throughput, and workforce constraints directly impact the delivery of critical infrastructure?  This session presents a practical case study from Smith Industries' Permian Basin operations, where AI-powered workflows, digital engineering platforms, and automation technologies are being applied across a multi-hundred-million-dollar portfolio supporting energy, utility, and digital infrastructure projects.  Attendees will learn how traditional paper-based fabrication processes were transformed into AI-enabled digital workflows using intelligent traveler systems, advanced 3D engineering tools, and data-driven quality controls. The session will examine the architecture and implementation decisions behind these systems, the challenges encountered during adoption, and the measurable operational outcomes achieved. Results include double-digit reductions in administrative effort, up to 40% less rework through digital engineering and design validation, and defect rates below 2% across product lines.  The talk will also explore how AI-assisted workflows and collaborative automation are being used to address skilled labor shortages, one of the most significant operational challenges in industrial fabrication today. Through digitally enabled welding systems and workflow automation, fabrication teams have achieved productivity gains of 2 to 3 times per shift while reducing rework by up to 50%.  Beyond the technology itself, the session will share lessons learned from deploying AI and automation in real production environments, including integration with existing processes, workforce adoption, scalability considerations, and measuring return on investment.  Attendees will leave with practical guidance for implementing AI toolkits, intelligent work processes, automated fabrication technologies, modular EPF and EPFC delivery models, and digitally connected supply chains managing more than $200 million in global procurement. The session concludes with key insights into the next phase of AI-enabled industrial manufacturing and infrastructure delivery.

Title: Building Event-Driven AI Agents for Proactive SAP Incident Management
Abstract: Modern SAP environments continuously generate operational events ranging from integration failures and interface exceptions to application errors and system alerts. Traditional monitoring platforms typically notify operators only after issues have already affected business operations, resulting in lengthy investigations and repetitive manual troubleshooting.  This session presents a practical event-driven multi-agent architecture that transforms SAP incident management from reactive monitoring into proactive, AI-assisted operations. Built on SAP Business Technology Platform, the solution uses autonomous agents that activate only when operational events occur. Individual agents collaborate to detect incidents, classify severity, identify likely root causes, retrieve historical resolutions and operational knowledge, and deliver contextual recommendations directly into Microsoft Teams through a purpose-built integration.  The presentation focuses on architectural patterns rather than products, covering event-driven agent activation, multi-agent coordination, contextual retrieval, recommendation workflows, observability, and human approval checkpoints before remediation actions are executed. It also explains why a custom Teams integration was chosen instead of a generic assistant connector, enabling richer notification logic, tailored escalation workflows, and operational conversations designed specifically for incident response.  Attendees will gain practical insights into designing reliable AI agent systems, integrating them with enterprise operations, and balancing automation with governance. The session concludes with implementation lessons, operational trade-offs, and reusable architectural patterns that engineering teams can adopt to build intelligent, scalable, and trustworthy AI-powered operational platforms.

Title: From Analytics to Action: Re-Architecting MDM for Agentic Enterprise AI
Abstract: Enterprise AI is moving beyond isolated text generation toward autonomous agents that can execute complex operational workflows, from real-time inventory placement to enterprise rewards orchestration. But most traditional data architectures were built for reporting and analytics, not for autonomous decision-making. In agentic systems, stale records, near-duplicate entities, inconsistent identifiers, or data drift can trigger serious downstream errors when decisions are executed directly across business-critical systems.  This session explores how Master Data Management must evolve for the agentic enterprise. Rather than serving only as a batch-processed analytics foundation, MDM must become an action-grade, immutable contract layer that supports reliable, real-time decisioning across operational workflows.  Drawing on experience building enterprise master data hubs, including a global system orchestration framework spanning 38,000 retail locations, the presentation will examine the architectural and strategic decisions required to create a stable data substrate for enterprise AI agents. Attendees will learn practical approaches for implementing sub-second match-and-survive functions, real-time routing, and event-driven orchestration using AWS Lambda, DynamoDB, and EventBridge.  The session will also cover idempotent workflow design, versioned data contracts, event-driven fan-out patterns, identity resolution strategies, and structural approaches for reducing data drift when autonomous agents interact with systems of record.  Designed for enterprise architects, data leaders, AI platform teams, and technology decision-makers, this session provides a practical blueprint for re-architecting MDM for action-oriented AI environments where data quality, entity resolution, and real-time routing directly shape operational outcomes.

Title: AI Agents for Hyper-Personalized Banking: Autonomous Financial Decision Systems
Abstract: AI agents are rapidly transforming how organizations automate complex decision-making and deliver personalized digital services. This session explores how autonomous AI agents can power hyper-personalized banking experiences by continuously analyzing real-time behavioral and transactional data. Instead of relying on static segmentation models, intelligent agents can proactively identify customer needs, recommend financial solutions, and dynamically adapt services based on evolving financial behavior.  The talk presents an architecture where AI agents interact with real-time data streams, predictive models, and financial service APIs to generate personalized recommendations such as savings strategies, credit options, and investment insights. These agents can continuously monitor customer interactions, evaluate contextual signals, and trigger adaptive financial “micro-products” tailored to individual needs.  The session also highlights governance considerations when deploying AI agents in regulated environments, including transparency, fairness, and data privacy protections. Attendees will gain practical insights into how agent-based AI systems can automate financial decision support, improve customer engagement, and enable scalable, intelligent financial platforms capable of delivering proactive and personalized banking experiences.

Title: From Health Data to Action: Building AI Agents That Observe, Reason, and Intervene
Abstract: Most personal health technology ends at the dashboard. It collects data, calculates a few metrics, and tells you what already happened.  AI agents make it possible to do something with that information.  In this talk, I’ll show how an agent can use data from wearables, phones, computers, and other personal data sources to look for patterns over time and decide when a small intervention, such as a notification, might actually be useful.  The important part is that the agent does not start from scratch every day. It keeps track of what it has seen before, what interventions it has tried, and what happened afterward. For example: Does staying on the computer late tend to be followed by worse sleep? If the agent sends a reminder to wind down, does the person actually do it? Does their sleep improve? And if it does not, should the agent try something different next time?  I’ll cover how to give the agent useful context and memory, keep analysis separate from action, limit what the agent is allowed to do, and evaluate whether its interventions seem to be helping. I’ll also talk about one of the biggest practical problems with this kind of system: preventing it from becoming an annoying notification generator that thinks every pattern it finds is meaningful.  The goal is not to build an AI doctor. The goal is to show how an agent can move beyond answering prompts and become a system that watches what happens in the real world, takes small actions, learns from the results, and changes what it does over time.  Attendees will leave with a practical architecture they can adapt to their own projects, whether they are working on health, productivity, behavior change, or another setting where an agent can learn from the consequences of its own actions.

Title: From Drone to Decision: What It Takes for AI to Do Real Work in Farming
Abstract: Agriculture is a good test of whether AI can actually get things done. The advice has money attached, the environment is messy, and the person acting on it is standing in a field.  At Syngenta we built a system that turns drone imagery into decisions growers act on. Plant level observations from Taranis drone flights feed a chain of models served through Cropwise AI: environmental yield potential, economic optimum plant population, crop phenology, and a cumulative stress index for disease pressure. The output is a per field economic answer delivered to the sales representative, the retailer and the grower.  It ran a full season with five retailers across five US states, then switched to weekly disease reporting. It now runs unattended, rendering every report on a weekly schedule with nobody watching.  This talk is about what that took, and what it tells us about putting autonomy into this domain.  The multi step problem is real: orchestrating several models, external APIs, and live weather and field data, then turning the result into something a person will act on. The interesting design question was how much of that to make autonomous. We put the LLM in exactly one stage of five and kept the rest deterministic, because a recommendation has to be reconstructible. When a grower asks why one field was ranked above another, an agronomist has to be able to challenge a specific number and get a specific justification.  I will be concrete about what that bought us, what it cost in adaptability, and what broke in production: a dependency upgrade that silently produced zero output while every unit test stayed green, and a data source returning success while dropping three quarters of its payload.  Then the forward question, which is the one I find most interesting: which parts of this pipeline are ready to hand to an agent, what has to be true before that is safe in a domain where money follows the advice, and what we are building next.

Title: The Retry Storm That Ate My Budget: Debugging the Hidden Cost Loops in Agentic AI
Abstract: Your agent works. It also just blew through $400 in tokens because it got stuck in a reasoning loop at 2 AM and nobody was watching. This talk is a technical deep-dive into the failure modes that silently drain your infrastructure budget when running agents in production — retry storms, runaway tool calls, context window bloat, and multi-agent orchestration overhead. I'll walk through real architectures where agents went off the rails, show you what the observability gaps looked like, and share the circuit-breaker patterns, token budgeting strategies, and cost-aware orchestration designs that brought things back under control. If you're building agents that run autonomously, this talk might save you a very awkward conversation with finance. Key Takeaways: How to identify and instrument the five most expensive failure modes in agentic architectures Circuit-breaker and token budgeting patterns that prevent runaway agent costs without killing autonomy A cost-aware orchestration design that routes between agent complexity levels based on task economics

Title: Reduce AI Agents Costs and Mistakes with Semantic tool Selection
Abstract: AI agents with many tools face a dual problem: they pick the wrong tool and waste tokens because tool descriptions get serialized into the context on every call. As agents scale to 50+ tools, errors increase and costs explode.  Semantic tool selection filters tools before they reach the LLM context using vector search, reducing errors and token costs.   This talk walks you through building TWO versions of the same travel agent to prove semantic tool selection works. By comparing the agents side-by-side on identical queries, you'll see dramatic improvements in both accuracy and cost and learn how to implement dynamic tool filtering that preserves conversation memory across multi-turn sessions.   You'll leave with working Python code and production patterns you can deploy immediately.

Title: A Unified Readiness Framework for Mission-Critical AI Agents and Autonomous Platforms
Abstract: Enterprise AI agent platforms increasingly integrate foundation models, retrieval systems, orchestration frameworks, cloud infrastructure, security services, enterprise applications, and human-in-the-loop workflows, requiring coordinated readiness across multiple technical and operational domains. However, organizations frequently evaluate these capabilities independently, resulting in fragmented governance, inconsistent deployment decisions, and increased operational risk. This paper presents the Mission-Critical Readiness Framework (MCRF) as a unified governance model for AI agent ecosystems, integrating technical, operational, infrastructure, security, organizational, and AI-specific readiness into a comprehensive lifecycle framework. MCRF establishes standardized readiness principles, measurable governance mechanisms, and structured assessment processes that evaluate agent reliability, model governance, tool connectivity, workflow resilience, observability, compliance, and operational preparedness before production deployment. By providing a common readiness model across engineering, AI, platform, security, and operations teams, the framework improves collaboration, strengthens governance, and enables evidence-based decisions throughout the AI agent lifecycle. As organizations deploy increasingly autonomous and interconnected intelligent systems, MCRF offers a practical, scalable, and repeatable methodology for achieving predictable, measurable, and trustworthy readiness across mission-critical AI agent platforms while improving delivery confidence, operational resilience, and long-term system reliability.

Title: From Scripted to Smart: How to Systematically Humanize Your AI Sales Agent
Abstract: Most AI sales agents don’t underperform because of weak models — they underperform because no one is measuring the right things in production. Accuracy benchmarks look fine, yet buyers disengage. The gap? We’re not evaluating conversational quality at the interaction level.  This talk is a technical deep dive into building human-like AI sales agents using LLM evals, production telemetry, and observability frameworks like LangSmith (and similar tooling). We’ll show how to move beyond static prompt tuning and into measurable, iterative system optimization.  You’ll learn how to:  Design multi-turn evals that measure flow, intent alignment, and adaptive verbosity  Use pairwise and win-rate evaluations to detect regressions in human-likeness  Instrument production systems to track AI detection signals (verbosity spikes, context resets, over-structuring)  Leverage tools like LangSmith to trace conversations, label failure modes, and connect evals to real revenue outcomes  Close the loop between offline evaluation and live performance using production conversation data  We’ll cover concrete metrics such as tokens-per-resolved-intent, clarification efficiency ratio, and state-progress efficiency — and how to operationalize them inside your LLM stack.  If you’re building AI agents in high-stakes sales environments, this session provides a practical framework for turning evals and observability into a competitive advantage — and systematically transforming scripted bots into adaptive, revenue-driving systems.

Title: Agentic Text-to-SQL in Production: What 500+ Data Marts and 30M Users Taught Us About LLM Orchestration
Abstract: Everyone demos text-to-SQL agents. Almost nobody runs them in production at national scale. This talk shares hard-won lessons from building and operating an on-prem NL2SQL platform serving 30M+ users across 500+ data marts with open-weight LLMs.  We'll cover the three parts of the agentic architecture that decided whether it worked: schema retrieval and routing across hundreds of marts, SQL generation with self-correction loops, and guardrails against hallucinated queries. I'll also be honest about what didn't work — where agent autonomy breaks down, and why bigger models didn't always win.  Target audience: data engineers, platform engineers, and anyone moving an LLM agent from demo to dependable enterprise infrastructure.

Title: Who Judges the AI Agent? LLM-as-Judge for Testing Non-Deterministic Code Generation
Abstract: Testing a deterministic API is straightforward — send input, assert output. Testing an AI agent is a different problem entirely. When your product ships an agentic system that takes natural language and generates executable code through a chain of tool calls, traditional assertions break down fast. Correctness has three dimensions that no single tool can cover alone.  In this talk, Liran Yushinsky, Automation Rockstar at JFrog AppTrust, shows how to built a three-layer evaluation framework for exactly this problem:  Deterministic — validate that AI-generated code compiles and conforms to the expected structure against the real API. LLM-as-judge — grade semantic alignment and completeness using another LLM as the evaluator, scoring output against a golden dataset of 30+ natural language to code reference pairs. Red-team — automatically scan the agent for prompt injection resistance using Garak, blocking any output that bypasses the agent's intended behavior  The result: a CI/CD gate that blocks merges when semantic alignment drops below threshold, syntax validity regresses, or any prompt injection test fails — fully automated, running on every PR that touches the agent's system prompt or tool configuration.  Key Takeaways:  * Why each layer catches failures the other two cannot — and why all three are required  * How to implement LLM-as-judge at scale with Promptfoo and Helicone, including practical scoring thresholds and golden dataset design  * How to wire all three layers into a CI/CD gate that blocks on AI quality regressions, not just unit test failures

Title: The Riskiest Agent in the Building: Profiling 100,000 Production Agents by Their Actions
Abstract: Most of what the industry knows about AI agent behavior comes from benchmarks, red team exercises, and architectural taxonomies. These measure what agents can do under test conditions. Yet, they tell very little about what agents actually do once they run real work, across real teams, with real permissions, tools, and data.  We observed over 100,000 active production agents, spanning coding agents, copilots, custom-built agents, and multi-agent systems, across enterprise environments over a six-month window. We tracked their behavior, tool usage, and confirmed risk events, then asked: which agent characteristics are actually associated with risky behavior?  In this talk, we will share which agent archetypes and tool combinations are most associated with real risk events, what those events consist of, and how they cluster into broader categories of risk. We will cover the methodology and its limitations, the platforms observed, and where our initial assumptions about what "risky" looks like turned out to be wrong.

Title: I Don't Trust AI Agents (And Neither Should You): Building Production-Ready Architectures
Abstract: Your AI agent works great in the demo. Then you deploy it and it hallucinates a refund policy that costs you $10K, or exposes customer data, or just loops endlessly burning tokens.  This session explores how to build AI agents you can trust in production using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and the Strands Agents SDK.  We’ll walk through a layered approach to agent safety that spans guardrails at multiple levels, including input validation, output filtering, and action approval, along with observability patterns that make agent behavior transparent and auditable.  You’ll also see how multi-agent architectures can be designed so agents steer and check one another, and how security policies combined with deliberate prompt design reduce risk across the system.  We'll walk through a reference architecture that combines these layers, and you'll learn how each layer can catch failures.  You should have basic familiarity with LLMs and AI agents. You'll leave with architectures pattern you can adapt and a clearer picture of what can go wrong and how to address common issues with AI agent trust and reliability.

Title: The Fairness Paradox: Why Your Compliant ML Model May Be Causing the Most Harm
Abstract: AI fairness regulations are tightening globally — but passing a disparate impact audit may not be enough. This talk introduces the Dollar-Cost Fairness Framework, developed through FairLens: an open-source credit-decisioning analysis tool built on 95,588 real HMDA mortgage applications.  We trained and evaluated 10 machine learning models — from logistic regression to neural networks — measuring not just accuracy, but the dollar-denominated harm imposed on protected groups. The findings are striking: a Support Vector Machine and a Neural Network achieved near-identical AUC scores, yet the SVM imposed $227M more in disparate harm against Black and Hispanic applicants. That is a 13x difference in financial harm between two "equally accurate" models.  We will walk through: - Why accuracy metrics systematically obscure fairness gaps in high-stakes lending - How Dollar-Cost Fairness translates model bias into regulatory and business risk ($) - AIF360 bias intervention techniques (reweighing, calibrated equalized odds) and their real tradeoffs - A live demo of FairLens showing model comparison, fairness dashboards, and bootstrap-validated results (p < 0.001)  Attendees will leave with a reusable evaluation framework, concrete code patterns for integrating fairness audits into ML pipelines, and a clearer picture of what "AI agent risk" means when agents are making financial decisions about people's lives.  This talk is for ML engineers, data scientists, and AI practitioners building or auditing decision systems — especially in regulated domains like finance, insurance, or hiring.

Title: RAGged and Compromised: Hacking Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation makes AI applications more useful, but it also creates a new security boundary: retrieved content becomes part of the model’s working context. In this session, we will intentionally break a simple RAG application using synthetic data and safe demos. We will look at direct prompt injection, poisoned documents, broken document-level authorization, unsafe tool use, insecure output handling, and data leakage through logging and citations.  Then we will rebuild the app with practical mitigations: identity-aware retrieval, document provenance, ingestion scanning, prompt isolation, source attribution, output validation, scoped tools, human approval for sensitive actions, and automated adversarial tests. The goal is not to scare people away from RAG, but to show how to design RAG apps as real enterprise systems with trust boundaries, policy enforcement, and observable controls.

Title: When Agents Decide: Accountability, Architecture and the Humans Left Holding the Liability
Abstract: Agentic AI is executing decisions faster than governance can follow. The accountability gaps it leaves behind are not hypothetical, and they were largely built in at the design stage.  The Case Agentic AI is no longer a research concept. It books travel, executes trades, screens job applicants, approves credit, and manages customer interactions, often with no human reviewing the individual decision before it is made. 2025 was the year the technology arrived. 2026 is the year organisations are discovering what they actually authorised.  The accountability problem is not subtle. When an agentic system causes harm, whether that is a discriminatory hiring decision, a wrongful credit refusal, or a safety-critical failure, the question of who is responsible is genuinely difficult to answer. The agent acted. No single human made the call. The decision may have emerged from a chain of micro-authorisations, none of which looked consequential at the time. Traditional liability frameworks were built on the assumption that a human made a decision and that a traceable chain of causation could be reconstructed. Agentic AI breaks both assumptions simultaneously.  The legal exposure is already crystallising. California AB 316, which took effect on 1 January 2026, explicitly forecloses the defence that an AI system's autonomous operation removes liability from the deployer. The EU's Product Liability Directive, due for implementation by December 2026, treats software including AI as a product subject to strict liability if found defective. Workday is currently facing a potential class action covering 1.1 billion job applications rejected by its AI screening tools. These are not regulatory abstractions. They are the downstream cost of governance decisions made, or not made, at the design and architecture stage.  Singapore's IMDA Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI, released at Davos in January 2026, introduced the concept of Meaningful Human Control, defined as the combination of human understanding, intervention capacity and traceability, precisely because existing frameworks were not designed for systems that can act, iterate and escalate permissions without human authorisation at each step. OWASP's Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 identifies agent goal hijacking, identity and privilege abuse, and cascading failures as the most critical systemic risks. None of these are purely technology problems. They are governance problems that technical decisions either create or close.  This talk makes the case that the accountability gap in agentic AI sits partly with the engineers and architects who are making the scoping decisions that determine what the agent can touch, what it can escalate, and what it will never be asked to justify.  What Attendees Will Take Away A clear account of the current legal and regulatory landscape for agentic AI accountability, and specifically what it means for engineers and architects rather than compliance teams. A framework for auditing where accountability in their agentic systems is assumed rather than assigned. A practical understanding of the Meaningful Human Control concept and how to test whether it actually exists in a given system, or whether it has been designed out incrementally through a series of individually reasonable decisions. A set of questions to take back to their teams about permission architecture, escalation design, and the points at which human oversight breaks down.

Title: Don't Give the Agent a Shell: Tool and Identity Boundaries for AI Agents in Cloud Operations
Abstract: An AI agent that can inspect logs, call cloud APIs, run infrastructure commands, or trigger a deployment is no longer just answering questions. It is participating in production operations.  The easiest prototype gives the agent a shell and a broadly privileged credential. A safer architecture gives it a small set of typed tools, a deliberately limited identity, and enforcement that sits outside the model.  This talk presents a practical design for cloud operations agents using patterns already used to secure CI/CD automation: separate identities for observation and execution, read-only access by default, short-lived credentials through workload identity federation, and state-changing actions placed behind plan, policy, and approval stages.  It will also cover failure modes that access control alone cannot prevent, including invalid tool arguments, repeated or partial execution, unsafe retries, timeouts, and missing audit context. Every tool call should be recorded as a production change event, with the agent identified as the actor.  Finally, the talk examines prompt injection through operational data. Logs, tickets, alert descriptions, and commit messages may contain attacker-controlled text, so agents must treat them as untrusted data rather than instructions.  These patterns come from securing privileged automation in real cloud environments. The principle throughout is simple: an agent's capability is defined by its tools and credentials. Keep both small.  Cloud operations agents should not receive an unrestricted shell and a powerful service account. This talk covers typed tools, split read and execute identities, short-lived credentials, plan-first actions, policy-enforced approvals, safe retries, complete auditing, and defences against prompt injection through logs and tickets.
